2. **The S&P matches lean flat to lower, and the risk is in the tails.** 3 of the 10 fell more than 17% within six months: 1966, Dec 2019 (into the Covid crash) and Oct 1987. On the other side, ordinary 4–7% pullbacks recovered about 75% of the time.
3. **The two indices point to different years.** The Nasdaq's best match is **October 1998**, which was followed by +51% in six months during the final blow-off. The S&P's best match is just *after* the 2000 top. In 1998–2000 the two moved together, so both analogs can't play out. That conflict is the clearest sign not to lean on any single match.
4. **Rough ranges for the next six months** (middle half of the matches, 25th to 75th percentile):
   - **S&P: about 6,850–7,500.** The median, about 7,200, stays below the high.
   - **Nasdaq: about 23,600–28,300.** The median is about 26,650.
5. **Levels to watch:**
   - **S&P −10% from its high, about 7,040.** In 2000 the first pullback bottomed at −11%, and ordinary pullbacks rarely go much past this level.
   - **S&P −20%, about 6,255.** That would be a bear market. In 2000 it took almost a year to get there.

Rates are the main risk outside these numbers. The 10-year yield is above 5%, and in 1999–2000 rising yields came before the top.
